en: The Ritual Manual for the Ordination of Going Forth and Receiving Full Acceptance (*Upasampadā-karmavācanā-vidhi*), with Brief Methods for Bhikṣu Training,
compiled by the Imperial Preceptor Bhikṣu Balha Sipa;
Homage to the Omniscient One.
Whenever there is one who wishes to seek ordination,
they may go at their own convenience to a teacher;
the teacher should then inquire regarding all obstructing factors.
One should ask in this manner:
"Are you not a follower of an external path?
Are you not less than fifteen years of age?"
Although you have reached fifteen years of age, is it not the case that you cannot frighten crows?
Although you can frighten crows, is it not the case that you are less than seven years old?
Are you not a slave or the like?
Are you not in debt? Have your parents not given their permission?
Even if your parents have not given their permission, are you not from a distant region?
Do you have no illness? Are you not a defiler of bhikṣuṇīs?
Are you not one who dwells as a thief?
Are you not one living apart?
Are you not one with whom one does not dwell together?
Are you not one who has been expelled?
Are you not a eunuch?
Are you not a magically conjured being? Are you not an animal?

Are you not one who has gone over to the non-Buddhist sects? Have you not previously been a member of a non-Buddhist sect, having already left the home life, only to return to that sect and come here once again?
Are you not one who has killed his mother?
Are you not one who has killed his father?
Have you not killed an Arhat? Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Have you not, with a malicious mind, drawn blood from the body of a Buddha?
Have you not committed any of the four *pārājika* offenses?
Have you not been expelled by the community for failing to confess an offense after committing one?
Are you not a person with a withered hand or otherwise deficient in your limbs and joints?
Are you not one with yellow hair and so forth?
Are you not one with deformed nails and so forth?
Are you not one excluded by the king and so forth?
"Are you not one whom the king has forbidden?
Even if you are not one whom the king has forbidden, are you not from a distant region?
Are you not one notorious as a robber?"
Are you not a person who harms others with poison?
Are you not a leather-worker? Are you not a butcher?
Are you not of a base or low-born lineage?
Are you not a non-human being?
Are you not a person from Uttarakuru?
"Are you not someone who has been repeatedly transferred from one family to another?
Are you not a woman with the appearance of a man?
Are you not a person of coarse or lowly appearance?"
"Are you not a person from another province with a different appearance?
When asking about obstructing factors regarding the Dharma,
if they say "yes," one may then reply:
Go as you please. If he is pure, he should be accepted;
you may then bestow upon him the lay follower's (upāsaka) vows of discipline.
When conferring [the precepts] in this manner, one first instructs the seeker of renunciation to first perform three prostrations to the Buddha,
followed by three prostrations to the preceptor (ācārya).
Squatting before him with palms joined,
he was instructed to say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me."
I, [Name], from this moment until the end of my life,
take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings.
I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire;
I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among all assemblies.
May the Venerable One bear witness.
"For as long as I live, I am an upāsaka.
Thus he says three times, up to the third repetition.
One should say, "The ācārya has realized it.
The teacher says, "Excellent.
The disciple replies, "Well said."
This concludes the conferral of the upāsaka vows.
Next, the instruction on the five precepts of the upāsaka is given, saying:
"Repeat after me."
Ācārya, please attend to me.
Just as the noble Arhats, for as long as they lived,
abandoned the taking of life.
I abstain from taking life.
I, [name], shall do likewise,
from this moment until the end of my life.
Abandoning the taking of life and abstaining from the taking of life—
this is the first limb;
it is the training precept of the noble Arhats.
I shall train myself accordingly, act accordingly,
and maintain this accordingly. Furthermore, as long as they live,
the noble Arhats abandon stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech.
Fruit-based fermented liquors and distilled spirits that cause intoxication and the derangement of one's nature are occasions for heedlessness;
one should even distance oneself from such fruit-based fermented liquors and distilled spirits that cause intoxication, the derangement of one's nature, and heedlessness.
I, [Name], shall do likewise.
From this moment until the end of my life,
I renounce theft, sexual misconduct, and false speech.
This is the place where fruit spirits and fermented liquors are brewed, which cause intoxication, confusion of nature,
and heedlessness. These five branches of training are the precepts studied by all the noble Arhats.
"I shall study, practice, and uphold [this] accordingly.
The teacher says, "Excellent.
The student replies, "Very well."
This concludes the ritual procedure for the upāsaka.
Next, one bhikṣu should be appointed to announce the matter to the assembly.
He should ask his preceptor as follows:
"Have all obstacles and hindrances already been inquired about?
"They have been inquired about," he replied.
"If they have been inquired about, that is well."
If one makes a formal announcement (jñapti) without having first asked for permission,
one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Next, one should make the announcement to the assembly.
The entire Saṃgha must assemble; alternatively, one may notify them by visiting their quarters.
Next, having led [the candidate] into the midst of the assembly and performed the rites of salutation, [the procedure continues].
Crouching before the elder and joining his palms,
he spoke as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please attend to me."
This person, so-and-so, seeks to go forth from the householder’s life under the preceptor, so-and-so;
he is still a layman in white robes and has not yet shaved his hair and beard.
"I wish to go forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya.
This person, [Name], desires to go forth, shave off hair and beard,
don the dyed robes, and give rise to right faith."
Having left the home life for the homeless state,
I seek to go forth from the preceptor [named] so-and-so.
"Is it permitted for the Saṃgha to allow so-and-so to go forth, given that he is free from obstacles and impediments and is of pure conduct?
The assembly all replied: "It is permitted."
If he is pure, he should be granted ordination;
if both [the candidate and the preceptor] have inquired, it is well.
If one does not inquire in this manner,
one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
This concludes the ritual procedure for informing the Saṃgha regarding those who have gone forth.
Next, regarding the request to be a preceptor (*upādhyāya*):
having paid homage to the preceptor (*ācārya*), one squats with palms joined and speaks as follows.
Venerable Ācārya, please attend to me. I, [name], now request you,
Ācārya, to be my Upādhyāya.
"I pray that the Ācārya will act as my Upādhyāya; because the Ācārya acts as the Upādhyāya, I shall go forth.
Thus he says three times.
Upon reaching the third repetition, one should say: "Because the preceptor acts as the preceptor.
The teacher says, "Well done."
He replied, "Excellent.
This concludes the ritual for requesting the upādhyāya.
Next is the procedure for requesting a bhikṣu to oversee the shaving of the hair.
He then shaved them all off.
The man later regretted it.
The Buddha said:
"One should leave a small amount of hair on the crown of the head. He asked,
"Is the topknot on your crown to be removed?"
If they say "no," you should say,
"Go as you please. If they say "remove it," [you should act accordingly].
One should shave [the hair] first, then provide a bath;
if it is cold, give warm water and offer cool water.
Next, the preceptor should provide him with an alms-bowl and the dyed robes;
having touched the preceptor’s feet to his own head, he may then receive the bowl and the robes.
Next, when the preceptor is about to give the robes and the lower garment to him to wear,
he must examine him,
fearing that he might be one who lacks sexual organs, possesses both sets of organs, or is otherwise incomplete.
This concludes the initial ritual procedure.
Next, the three refuges are conferred,
as well as the going forth from the household life.
First, have them pay homage to the Buddha;
next, have them pay homage to their preceptor.
Then, have them squat and join their palms.
Instruct them to speak as follows:
"Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me.
I, [name], from this moment until the end of my life, take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings."
I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire;
I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the most honored among all assemblies.
That Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni—the Lion of the Śākyas, the King of the Śākyas—is our supreme honor.
Once he has gone forth,
I shall follow him in going forth,
casting aside my worldly appearance and assuming the outward form of one who has left the household life.
"I am currently upholding it.
I am now correctly proceeding toward it.
Thus he says three times.
Upon reaching the third repetition, one should say: "I have come for a specific purpose to state my name;
my preceptor's name is so-and-so."
The Master says, "Excellent.
The disciple replies, "Virtuous.
This concludes the ritual protocol for leaving the household life.
Next, the preceptor should assign a bhikṣu to act as the preceptor for bestowing the śrāmaṇera vows;
that bhikṣu should then question the preceptor.
How can this person be one who is completely pure?
If he were completely pure,
he should have become a śrāmaṇera.
Next, having paid homage to the Buddha and the preceptor,
one should squat with palms joined and speak as follows.
Venerable sir, please attend to me.
I, [Name], from this moment until the end of my life,
take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings.
I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire;
I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the most honored among all assemblies.
May the Venerable One bear witness to this.
"For as long as life lasts, I am a śrāmaṇera.
Thus he says three times,
reaching the third repetition.
One should say: "I pray that the Ācārya will bear witness that for as long as I live, I am a śrāmaṇera.
The teacher says: "Excellent."
The response is: "Excellent.
This concludes the ritual for conferring the śrāmaṇera precepts.
Next, with the exception of the ācārya, one bhikṣu [should be appointed].
One should immediately measure the shadow to determine the *śaṅku* and finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
as well as the divisions of day and night and other such methods,
all in accordance with the procedures set forth in the *Bhikṣu-śīla*.
Next, the instruction for the ten precepts is conferred as follows: "Repeat after me:
'Venerable Ācārya, please attend to me.'"
Just as all noble Arhats, for as long as they live,
have abandoned killing and abstained from killing,
so too shall I, [name], do likewise.
From this moment until the end of my life,
I shall abandon taking life and remain far removed from killing.
This is the first limb.
This is the training ground of the noble Arhats;
I shall train in it, practice it, and maintain it accordingly.
Furthermore, as long as life endures for those noble Arhats...
He abandons stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech;
as well as fermented fruits, distilled liquors, and intoxicants that cause delusion and negligence;
and dancing, singing, music, perfumes, garlands, necklaces, and the application of cosmetics.
High beds, large beds, eating at improper times,
and the keeping of gold and silver— even unto the complete renunciation of keeping gold and silver—
I, [Name], shall likewise do.
From this moment until the end of my life,
I shall renounce stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech;
as well as the consumption of fermented fruits, spirits, and liquors that cause intoxication, mental derangement, and heedlessness.
Engaging in song, dance, and music; using perfumes, garlands, necklaces, and ointments;
using high beds and large couches; eating at improper times;
and possessing gold and silver—even to the point of being far removed from possessing gold and silver.
These ten branches of training are the training rules of all the noble Arhats; I shall train in them,
practice them, and maintain them accordingly.
The teacher says, "Excellent.
The student replies, "Virtuous.
This concludes the ritual procedure for bestowing the śrāmaṇera precepts.
The Ritual for Bestowing Full Ordination: If that person has reached twenty years of age, the preceptor (upādhyāya) should provide them with a request for a bowl, the three robes, and so forth.
Having invited the *karmavācanā*-master and the private instructor,
they enter the ritual enclosure;
when the assembly of *bhikṣus* has gathered together, [the procedure continues].
During that half-month,
while engaged in guarding, confessing, and maintaining [the precepts],
each person reflects upon it individually.
Having recognized one's transgressions,
one should first guard against them, confess them, maintain restraint, and cultivate purification;
only then should one sit.
If it is in a central land, one may assemble a group of ten or more;
if it is in a borderland, one may assemble a group of five or more together with a *vinayadhara*.
The recipient of the precepts must first pay homage to the Buddha three times;
next, they must pay homage to each member of the Sangha individually three times.
However, there are two kinds of reverence.
The first consists of the five points touching the ground: namely, the forehead-point, the two palms, and the two knees.
The second consists of holding the teacher’s calves and feet with both hands while walking at one's own pace.
Once one has paid respects to the first,
one should request the upādhyāya to first pay homage and place a brick or a pottery shard upon it, with grass spread over it.
The one receiving the precepts should squat upon it with palms joined;
if he was previously an upādhyāya [of the candidate], [he should remain so].
Or it may be spoken at any time by an ācārya; however,
if one was not previously one of the two teachers, [it must be said at the proper time].
One should address them as "Venerable Sir" (bhadanta) or "Reverend" (āyuṣmat).
If one is requesting the preceptor (upādhyāya), [one should say:]
One should act accordingly.
Maintaining proper deportment,
one should speak as follows:
Venerable sir, please attend to me.
I, [name], now request the venerable one to be my upādhyāya.
May the venerable one act as my upādhyāya.
"Because the Venerable One is my upādhyāya, I shall receive full ordination.
Thus it is said three times, until the third repetition.
At that point, one should say: "Because the Venerable One is my upādhyāya, [I shall receive full ordination]."
When conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*),
the preceptor says, "Excellent," and the candidate replies, "Well said."
This concludes the ritual procedure for requesting the upādhyāya.
Next, the preceptor, the upādhyāya,
should consecrate the three dharma robes.
If these are robes that have been cut, sewn, and stitched,
one should empower them in this manner:
take the three dharma-robes.
Have each person fold [the robe] and place it together upon the left shoulder of that person.
Afterwards, the preceptor and the candidate for ordination rise together.
The candidate for ordination should hold the corners of the saṃghāṭī with both hands—translated as the "repeatedly layered robe"—and it should be spoken thus:
Venerable Upādhyāya, please bear me in mind:
I, [name], have already completed this robe,
which is fit and worthy to be accepted.
I now formally accept this Dharma robe as my saṃghāṭī.
Thus he spoke three times.
The teacher said, "Excellent.
He replied, "Virtuous."
Next, holding the corners of the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) with both hands— translated as the "inner garment"—
one should speak thus:
"Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me."
I, [Name], have already completed this robe;
it is fit and suitable for use as an *uttarāsaṅga*. I now formally accept and maintain it.
Thus it was said three times.
The teacher said, "Excellent.
The respondent said, "Virtuous."
Next, holding the *antaravāsa*— translated as "inner garment"— with both hands,
one should speak thus:
"Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me."
I, [Name], have already completed this robe;
it is fit for use as an *antarvāsa*. I now formally accept and maintain it.
Thus it was said three times.
The teacher replied, "Excellent.
[The student] answered, "Very well. This is the ritual procedure for maintaining, cutting, and sewing the three robes.
If there are no robes already cut and sewn,
one should maintain and consecrate a bolt of cloth;
at that time, both persons should rise together.
Take three articles and,
having folded each one separately, place them together over the person's left shoulder,
holding them as the corners of a saṃghāṭī robe.
It should be spoken thus:
"Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me.
This robe, [named] so-and-so, is for the purpose of a saṃghāṭī robe."
I now maintain this vow:
if there are no obstacles or difficulties, I shall make robes of nine strips and so forth,
as well as those with two lengths and one short strip.
I shall wash, spread out, cut, patch, hem, sew, and dye it;
or I shall apply patches upon it,
so that this robe may be fit for use.
"This is fit for use.
Thus he says three times.
The teacher replies, "Excellent."
He replies, "Excellent.
Next, holding it as the corner of the *uttarāsaṅga*,
he should speak as follows:
Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me.
This robe, [name], is for the *uttarāsaṅga*;
I now formally accept it.
If there are no obstacles or difficulties,
one should fashion a Dharma robe consisting of seven strips— two long and one short—
and then dye, wash, spread out, cut, patch, sew, or apply supplementary patches upon it.
"This robe may be used according to its suitability; it is fit to be utilized.
Thus he says three times.
The preceptor says, "Good.
The candidate replies, "Virtuous.
Next, holding the material for the *antarvāsa* robe, he should speak thus: "O Upādhyāya, please attend to me."
I, [Name], shall use this object as an *antarvāsa*.
I now formally take possession of it,
provided there are no obstacles.
I shall make five-strip *antarvāsa* dharma robes,
with two pieces long and one short;
I shall dye, wash, spread out, cut, patch, mark with lines, and sew them.
Or, having patched it upon the upper part,
this robe may be used as appropriate; it is fit to be utilized.
Thus it was said three times.
The teacher said, "Excellent.
The respondent said, "Virtuous."
This concludes the section on the observance of the three robes (*tricīvara*) that have never been cut or trimmed.
The ritual protocol for the three robes is finished.
Next, the bowl should be presented to the community of monks.
Then, one bhikṣu shall hold the bowl in his left palm and cover the opening of the bowl with his right hand.
One should personally approach each monk,
starting from the senior-most elder, and speak as follows,
addressing them as "Venerable Sir" (*bhadanta*).
Or one may say: "Venerable sir, please attend;
does this *pāṭala* belonging to the venerable [so-and-so] not count as small?"
"Is it not large?
Is it not white?"— one should ask in this manner.
If there are no obstacles or difficulties,
the assembly may all say "Excellent.
If they say "Excellent," it is well.
If one does not speak thus, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
This concludes the ritual procedure for displaying the bowl.
Next, the upādhyāya should personally consecrate the pātra.
It should be performed in this manner:
together with the person receiving the precepts, they arise simultaneously;
the two hold the alms bowl together with their left hands.
Each person should cover the mouth of their bowl with their right hand and be instructed to say:
"Venerable Upādhyāya, please attend to me."
I, [Name], this pātra is fit for use as food;
it is a worthy vessel.
This is the vessel of the Great Sage;
it is the vessel for alms-gathering.
I now receive and maintain it.
Thus it was said three times.
The teacher said, "Excellent.
The disciple replied, "Virtuous."
This concludes the ritual procedure for maintaining the *pātra*.
Next, one should bestow the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and the water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*).
Following that, one should give him the *saṃghāṭī* robe to wear.
Instruct them to pay homage to the assembly of monks three times.
They should be placed where they can see [the monks] but not hear them.
Instruct them to stand with single-minded devotion, palms joined, facing the assembly with reverence.
The *karmavācanā* master should ask the assembly:
"Who among you has previously received an invitation from that preceptor [named] so-and-so?
You should go to a secluded place to provide instruction for the sake of [the candidate named] so-and-so."
The one who has accepted the invitation should reply,
"I, [Name]. Next, the *karmavācaka* (ceremonial master) should ask:
"O Bhikṣu [Name], with [Name] as your preceptor (upādhyāya),
are you able to instruct [Name] in a secluded place?"
He should reply, "I am able.
Next, the *karmavācanā* master shall take the *praśnavid* (questioner) aside to inquire about the obstacles and impediments.
Having performed the *jñapti-karman* (the motion),
the *karman-ācārya* (ceremonial master) shall sit down and speak as follows.
Venerable Saṃgha, please attend to me. This bhikṣu,
[Name], has [Name] as his upādhyāya.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they are willing to listen,
may the Saṃgha grant permission for [the teacher] to instruct [so-and-so] in a private place.
This bhikṣu, [name], with [name] as his upādhyāya,
has been instructed by [name] in a secluded place.
This is the announcement;
this is the appointment.
The procedure for the private instruction of the preceptor is hereby concluded.
Next, having privately instructed the bhikṣu, he should lead him to a secluded place.
Once he has been taught to perform prostrations and is crouching with palms joined,
he should speak as follows:
"Venerable one, listen.
This is the time for your sincerity; this is the time for your truthful speech.
I now have a few questions for you."
You should, with a mind free from fear,
say "it exists" if it exists,
or "it does not exist" if it does not.
"One must not speak falsely. Are you a man?
"He replies, 'I am. 'Do you possess the male organ?'"
He replied, "I possess them.
"Are you twenty years of age?
He replied, "I am."
"Do you possess the three robes and the alms bowl?
He replied, "I possess them.
"Are your parents still living?"
He replied, "Is he present? [The other] answered, "Yes. He asked again, "Does he permit your going forth?
[The other] answered, "He does. [He asked once more,] "Is he dead? [The other] answered, "He is."
There is no need to ask further:
"Are you not a slave?
Are you not a person who has been brought here by theft?"
Have you not come seeking profit and gain?
Are you not a person involved in disputes?
Are you not a person sold by others?
"Are you not someone selected for special service by the royal house?
Are you not someone employed out of fear by the royal house?
Are you not someone who inflicts harm upon the royal house?"
Have you not harmed the royal family yourself, or incited others to harm them?
Are you not known as a robber? Are you not a tax-evader?
Are you not a eunuch? Are you not one who has defiled a bhikṣuṇī?
Are you not one who dwells as a thief?
Are you not one living apart?
Are you not one with whom we do not dwell together?
Are you not a follower of another path? You are currently a follower of another path.

"Are you not one who has gone over to the non-Buddhist sects? Have you not previously been a member of a non-Buddhist sect, having already left the household life, only to return to that sect and come back here again?
Are you not one who has killed his father?
Are you not one who has killed his mother?"
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Have you not, with malicious intent, shed the blood of a Buddha?
"Are you not a magically conjured being? Are you not an animal?
One should ask these questions, and all should answer, "No.
"Do you not owe others a debt, whether small or large, or even a trifling amount?"
If one says that it exists, one should ask:
"Once you have conferred full ordination, will you be able to repay that debt?"
If you say you can, that is well.
If you say you cannot, you may ask those who have consented; only then should you come.
"Have you not previously gone forth?
If you say, 'I have previously gone forth,' you should be questioned."
"Have you not committed any of the four *pārājika* offenses?
When you returned to lay life, did you properly relinquish the precepts?
He replied, "I have committed a grave offense."
Go as you please.
If you have committed no offense, are you currently an ordained renunciant?
If you say that you are, [then...]
"Do you practice the holy life?
He replied, "I do.
The questioner asked:
"What is your name? He replies, "My name is so-and-so."
"Question: What is the name of your upādhyāya?
Answer: I shall state the name of my upādhyāya because of this matter;
the name of my upādhyāya is so-and-so."
Venerable sir, there are such diseases as these among human beings:
namely, leprosy, goiters, scrofula, pustules, ulcers,
vitiligo, and scabies.
Scabies and skin sores on the feet;
emaciation from wasting diseases and loss of the soul;
hunger and illness; cold-induced swelling.
Leprosy with chronic edema;
acute epidemics at their most severe stage;
or illnesses lasting for one or two days.
On the third and fourth days,
wind, yellow phlegm, and mucus congregate;
the illness diminishes one day and flares up the next.
Chronic illnesses and temporary ailments;
abscesses, carbuncles, and swellings; diseases of the throat and hiccups;
coughs, labored breathing, and tumors.
Pain and numbness in the hands and feet; various nodules and blood disorders;
carbuncles, hemorrhoids, and fistulas; nausea and vomiting;
and the debilitating affliction of dysuria.
There are fevers that pervade the entire body,
pain in the flanks, and aching in the bones and joints;
you have none of these ailments.
"And as for other ailments, are you free from them? He replied, "I am.
"Venerable one, listen."
Just as I am now questioning you in this private place,
so too shall the bhikṣus question you in the midst of the great assembly.
You should, in that place, maintain a mind free from fear.
If someone says "it exists," or if they say "it does not exist," one should answer truthfully.
"You should remain here for now;
do not come unless you are summoned.
This concludes the ritual protocol for instruction in a secluded place.
Next, having instructed a bhikṣu to go ahead on half the path,
he should stand facing the assembly with palms joined and speak as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
That such-and-such person has already been properly instructed by me in private;
I have questioned him regarding the obstructing factors.
"Such-and-such a person acts as the upādhyāya.
Is it permissible for him to come, provided he is pure?
The entire assembly replied, "If he is pure, then it is so."
"He should be summoned.
They all said, "Very well. "If he does not speak in this manner," [he should be brought].
One incurs an offense against the Dharma.
Next, one should call out from afar to summon them.
Once they have arrived among the assembly, they must first prostrate to the Sangha three times.
To receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*),
